title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026]
Title:$Ψ$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

report.summary: Ψ-0.6 is a unified vision-language world model that adaptively interleaves images, text, geometry and motion tokens inside a single, reinforcement-tuned reasoning process.
report.background: Most AI systems today are specialists: vision-language models describe images, dedicated geometry networks reconstruct 3D structure, and physics simulators roll out trajectories. Because these capabilities live in separate models with separate interfaces, they are hard to compose, and a system cannot switch reasoning style mid-problem the way a person does — sketching a diagram, doing mental rotation, then running a quick physical what-if. Chain-of-thought research has mostly pushed in the opposite direction, forcing all reasoning into text. Ψ-0.6, posted as an arXiv preprint (2610.32177, cs.AI), argues that a world model should instead choose its own representational substrate. It builds on trends in interleaved multimodal generation, spatial-reasoning benchmarks, and reinforcement learning from task feedback, and positions itself against leading open-weight vision-language models on zero-shot multi-view spatial tasks.
key_points: Streams of thought replace a single text chain: the model interleaves natural language, generated images, and explicit encodings of geometry and motion through one shared token interface, so it can both produce and read back each representation during a single reasoning pass.

On multi-view spatial reasoning the model beats leading open-weight systems zero-shot, and accuracy improves further when it reasons through geometric intermediates rather than jumping straight from question to answer, suggesting the intermediate format itself carries useful computation.

It supports counterfactual simulation: the model generates imagined scenes and then interprets them to answer questions like whether moving an object would block a pathway — a step beyond describing what is visible toward predicting what would happen.

Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly trains three things at once: which representation to pick, how to generate it, and how to use it. Gains in visual question answering transfer to unseen benchmarks, indicating the policy generalizes rather than overfitting one dataset.
report.impact: If the approach holds up, it shifts world models from passive predictors to active reasoners that decide how to think, not just what to answer. For the AI industry, that means the boundary between vision models, 3D reconstruction stacks, and simulators becomes a design choice inside one model rather than an integration problem — a challenge to pipelines glued together with APIs. For developers, the interesting artifact is the shared token interface: a template for letting models emit structured intermediates (poses, meshes, motion) that other tools can consume. Regular users would feel this in embodied assistants and robotics, where asking 'what if I move this?' matters more than captioning. Caveats: this is a preprint with no peer review, and compute cost of generating images mid-reasoning may be high.
report.tools: Read the paper and its HTML version on arXiv (2610.32177) and follow discussion on alphaXiv. To experiment, study open-weight multimodal baselines such as Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL, geometry backbones like DUSt3R/VGGT for spatial tokens, simulators such as MuJoCo, Isaac Lab or Genesis for counterfactuals, and RL post-training frameworks like veRL or OpenRLHF for task-feedback tuning. Track the authors' Hugging Face page for weights or code releases.
